"The United States would like to see a restoration of normal deliveries," White House spokesman Gordon Johndroe said. "The parties should be resolving their differences through good-faith negotiations, without supply cutoffs." The frigid weather is of particular concern, the White House said. "We urge both sides to keep in mind the humanitarian implications of any interruption of gas supply in the winter," Johndroe said. Another part of the dispute centers on Gazprom's price hike for 2009 gas deliveries. Gazprom had wanted to more than double Ukraine's payments, but Wednesday it offered a lower price. Ukraine, which currently pays about $100 per 1,000 cubic meters, balked at the figure offered, saying it simply can't afford to pay the new price. It is the second time in three years Gazprom has threatened to cut off gas supplies to Ukraine. The company made good on its threat on January 1, 2006, but turned the supply back on a day later. Russia is the world's biggest producer of natural gas and supplies Europe with more than 40 percent of its imports -- mainly via the pipelines through Ukraine. Naftogaz said in its statement Thursday that it would ensure the uninterrupted flow of Russian gas to Europe through Ukraine, but only under existing arrangements. It indicated some gas deliveries to Europe could be halted in Ukraine if Naftogaz fails to reach a new agreement with Gazprom. Although gas is still flowing to Europe, there are also concerns in Russia that the amount could be reduced if Ukraine siphons off some of the gas headed to the west. Naftogaz said it will continue negotiating with Gazprom to address the issues.

“All of Ukraine’s consumers are fully secured,” the company said in a statement.

MOSCOW, Russia (CNN) — Gazprom, Russia’s state-dominated energy giant, announced Thursday that it had stopped sending natural gas to Ukraine after a deadline for payment passed.

The company, which had previously warned it might take this step, said repeated negotiations with Ukraine over unpaid bills had not produced a solution. Gazprom says Ukraine owes roughly $2 billion for earlier gas deliveries.

The dispute also involves the price Gazprom set for gas shipments in 2009. That rate was initially more than twice the 2008 price, and Ukraine has challenged it.

Gazprom has told other European countries that their gas deliveries, which pass through pipelines in Ukraine, will not be disrupted by the disagreement with Kiev. On Thursday, a Gazprom representative said on Russian state television that supplies to the rest of Europe had actually been increased.

“Gazprom will continue supplying gas for its consumers in Europe at full volume,” said Alexey Miller, the company’s chief executive. “We have an effective transit contract.”

The cutoff could leave some Ukrainians facing very cold conditions. At midday Thursday, the temperature in Kiev was 25 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 4 degrees Celsius, with the day’s high expected to reach only 32 F, or 0 C, and snow forecast overnight.

Ukraine’s state-controlled energy firm, Naftogaz Ukrainy, said Thursday that it was meeting the country’s domestic gas requirements by drawing from underground storage sites.

“All of Ukraine’s consumers are fully secured,” the company said in a statement.

In Washington, the White House called for the disagreement to be settled.

“The United States would like to see a restoration of normal deliveries,” White House spokesman Gordon Johndroe said. “The parties should be resolving their differences through good-faith negotiations, without supply cutoffs.”

The White House also emphasized the danger posed by the severe winter weather.

“We urge both sides to keep in mind the humanitarian implications of any interruption of gas supply in the winter,” Johndroe said.

Naftogaz Ukrainy rejected Gazprom’s allegation that it still owed money for previous supplies. The Ukrainian company said Thursday that it had fully paid its debt to Gazprom, although it did not provide a specific amount.

Another major disagreement concerns Gazprom’s proposed 2009 price increase. The Russian company had sought to raise Ukraine’s payments by more than double, but on Wednesday it proposed a reduced rate. Ukraine, which now pays about $100 per 1,000 cubic meters, rejected the offer, saying it could not afford the new price.

This is the second time in three years that Gazprom has threatened to suspend gas shipments to Ukraine. It followed through on a similar warning on January 1, 2006, but resumed supplies the next day.

Russia is the largest natural gas producer in the world and provides Europe with more than 40 percent of its gas imports, mostly through pipelines crossing Ukraine.

Naftogaz said Thursday that it would maintain the uninterrupted transit of Russian gas to Europe through Ukrainian territory, but only according to current agreements. The company suggested that some Europe-bound gas shipments could be stopped inside Ukraine if it does not reach a new deal with Gazprom.

While gas continues to reach Europe, Russian officials are concerned that volumes could fall if Ukraine diverts some of the gas intended for western customers.

Naftogaz said it would keep holding talks with Gazprom in an effort to resolve the dispute.

counterfactuals.output:
**Gazprom cuts off gas supplies to Ukraine amid debt and pricing dispute**

**Kyiv, Ukraine (CNN)** — Russian energy giant Gazprom halted natural gas deliveries to Ukraine on Monday after talks failed to resolve a bitter dispute over unpaid bills and the price Kyiv should pay for future supplies, raising fresh concerns about energy security in Europe.

Gazprom said it moved Ukraine to a prepayment system after the country’s state gas company, Naftogaz, failed to pay outstanding debts. Under the new arrangement, Ukraine will receive Russian gas only for volumes paid for in advance, the company said.

“From today, the Ukrainian company will receive Russian gas only in the amounts it has paid for,” Gazprom said in a statement, accusing Naftogaz of failing to settle billions of dollars in arrears.

Naftogaz rejected Gazprom’s terms, saying the price demanded by Moscow was politically motivated and far above market levels. The Ukrainian company said it remained ready to continue negotiations but would not accept what it described as an unfair price increase imposed after months of political tension between Kyiv and Moscow.

The cutoff does not immediately stop Russian gas flowing to Europe through pipelines that cross Ukraine, Gazprom said. But the dispute has renewed fears of disruptions for European customers, many of whom depend on Russian gas transported via Ukrainian territory.

The European Union urged both sides to return to talks and warned against any action that could threaten supplies to EU member states. European officials have been mediating negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv, seeking a compromise on Ukraine’s debt and a temporary gas price.

“The priority is to ensure that gas transit to Europe continues without interruption,” an EU official said, adding that the bloc was monitoring pressure levels and supply volumes closely.

The White House criticized Russia’s move, saying energy should not be used as a political weapon. U.S. officials called on Moscow and Kyiv to resolve the dispute through negotiations and said Ukraine’s energy security remained a priority for Washington and its allies.

The gas standoff comes against the backdrop of a broader crisis in relations between Russia and Ukraine following months of unrest, Russia’s annexation of Crimea, and continuing violence in eastern Ukraine.

Previous gas disputes between Russia and Ukraine led to major disruptions in Europe, particularly in 2006 and 2009, when supply cutoffs left several countries scrambling for alternative energy sources during winter. This time, European officials said storage levels and warmer weather could help cushion the immediate impact, but they warned that a prolonged shutdown could create serious problems later in the year.

Ukraine has said it can rely on stored gas and reverse-flow supplies from European neighbors in the short term, though analysts say the country remains vulnerable if the dispute drags on.

For now, the cutoff marks a new escalation in the economic confrontation between Moscow and Kyiv — and another test of Europe’s ability to shield its energy system from the fallout of the Ukraine crisis.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

**MOSCOW, Jan. 1, 2009** — Russia’s state-controlled gas monopoly Gazprom halted natural gas deliveries to Ukraine on Thursday after a payment deadline expired without agreement in a bitter debt and pricing dispute, raising fresh concerns about energy supplies to Europe during the winter heating season.

Gazprom said it had stopped supplying gas intended for Ukrainian domestic consumption after Kyiv failed to settle outstanding debts and sign a new contract for 2009. The company said flows destined for European customers through pipelines crossing Ukraine would continue, but warned that Ukraine would be responsible for ensuring uninterrupted transit.

“Gas supplies to Ukraine have been reduced to zero,” Gazprom officials said, adding that transit volumes for Europe were being maintained at contracted levels.

Ukraine’s state energy company Naftogaz rejected accusations that it was failing to meet its obligations and accused Moscow of using energy as a political weapon. Ukrainian officials said they had made payments toward the debt and disputed additional penalties claimed by Gazprom. Kyiv also objected to Russia’s proposed price increase for gas in the new year, saying the demanded rate was excessive and not matched by transit fees paid to Ukraine for carrying Russian gas westward.

The dispute centers on billions of dollars in unpaid bills, late-payment penalties and disagreements over the price Ukraine should pay for Russian gas. Gazprom has said Ukraine owes more than $2 billion, including fines, while Naftogaz has disputed portions of the total and said negotiations were still possible.

The cutoff comes as much of Ukraine and Eastern Europe face freezing winter weather, increasing demand for heating fuel. Ukrainian authorities said the country had sufficient gas in underground storage to meet domestic needs in the short term, but analysts warned that a prolonged standoff could pressure supplies and heighten risks for downstream customers.

The European Union, which receives a significant share of its Russian gas imports through Ukrainian pipelines, urged both sides to resolve the dispute quickly and avoid any disruption to European consumers. Several EU states remain sensitive to interruptions after previous Russia-Ukraine gas disputes affected supplies in midwinter.

Gazprom insisted that it would continue to pump gas for Europe and said any shortfall would be the result of unauthorized withdrawals by Ukraine. Naftogaz denied it would siphon off transit gas and said it would fulfill its responsibilities as a transit country.

The confrontation reflects a recurring vulnerability in Europe’s energy system: dependence on Russian gas transported through Ukrainian infrastructure. While Russia has sought alternative export routes, Ukraine remains a critical corridor for supplies to Central and Western Europe.

Talks between Gazprom and Naftogaz broke down late Wednesday after both sides failed to agree on a new contract before the deadline. Russian officials said deliveries would resume only after Ukraine paid its debts and accepted market-based pricing. Ukrainian officials said they were prepared to continue negotiations but would not accept what they called “unjustified” terms.

With temperatures falling and the holiday period complicating diplomacy, European governments are watching closely for signs that the dispute could spread beyond Ukraine’s borders.

**Moscow Cuts Gas Supplies to Ukraine as Debt Dispute Raises Fears for Europe**

**MOSCOW/KIEV —** Russia’s state-controlled energy giant Gazprom has halted natural gas deliveries to Ukraine, escalating a bitter payment dispute with Kiev and reviving fears that the standoff could disrupt supplies to European consumers during a period of severe winter weather.

Gazprom said it had stopped deliveries after Ukraine failed to settle what Moscow describes as a major outstanding gas debt. Russian officials accused Kiev of repeatedly missing payment deadlines and warned that no further gas would be supplied without advance payment or a binding settlement.

Ukraine rejected the accusation that it is refusing to pay, insisting the debt figures cited by Moscow are inflated and politically motivated. Officials in Kiev said Ukraine has either paid for gas received or is contesting charges linked to disputed prices, penalties, and contract terms. The Ukrainian government accused Russia of using energy as leverage at a time of heightened political tension between the two neighbors.

The cutoff has immediate implications for Ukraine, which depends heavily on natural gas for heating, electricity generation, and industrial use. It also carries wider risks for Europe. A significant share of Russian gas bound for European Union countries traditionally moves through pipelines crossing Ukrainian territory. Any interruption, pressure drop, or unauthorized diversion along the transit network could affect supplies to Central and Eastern Europe and potentially beyond.

European officials urged both sides to keep commercial and political disputes separate from transit obligations. Energy authorities in several EU capitals said they were monitoring pipeline pressure and storage levels, while calling for transparency from both Moscow and Kiev. The European Commission has previously stressed that Russia must honor supply contracts with European buyers and that Ukraine must guarantee uninterrupted transit.

Gazprom warned that while gas intended for European customers would continue to be pumped into the Ukrainian transit system, Kiev would be responsible for ensuring it moved onward. Russian officials suggested that if shortages appeared in Europe, Ukraine would bear the blame. Ukrainian authorities denied any intention of taking transit gas and said Russia was manufacturing a crisis to undermine Kiev’s credibility as a reliable transit state.

The dispute comes amid freezing temperatures across parts of Ukraine, raising humanitarian concerns. Municipal authorities warned that prolonged supply reductions could strain district heating systems, particularly in older residential blocks, hospitals, schools, and shelters. Emergency planners said priority would be given to essential services, but acknowledged that local networks could face pressure if the cutoff continues.

Humanitarian groups expressed concern for vulnerable populations, including elderly residents, displaced families, and low-income households unable to afford alternative heating. In many Ukrainian cities, centralized heating systems rely on gas-fired plants, leaving communities exposed if fuel supplies tighten during cold weather.

Analysts say the conflict reflects a long-running pattern in Russia-Ukraine energy relations: disputes over pricing, debt, and political alignment have repeatedly spilled over into supply interruptions. Previous gas crises have led to temporary reductions in European deliveries, prompting the EU to expand storage capacity, diversify suppliers, and develop reverse-flow mechanisms that allow Ukraine to import gas from European neighbors.

Still, experts warn that winter conditions leave little room for miscalculation. Even if European storage levels are adequate, a prolonged confrontation could unsettle markets and push up prices. For Ukraine, the stakes are more immediate: conserving supplies, maintaining heating systems, and preventing a domestic energy emergency.

Diplomatic efforts are expected to intensify in the coming days, with European mediators likely to press for a temporary payment arrangement or monitored transit mechanism. But positions remain far apart. Moscow insists payment must come first. Kiev says it will not accept what it calls politically inflated bills.

For now, the gas dispute has become both an economic confrontation and a test of regional energy security — with millions of Ukrainians facing the cold and European governments watching anxiously for signs that the crisis could move beyond Ukraine’s borders.
